name: THE CHIMI-CHURRI YOU CAN'T BE SERIOUS BURGER

recipe.history:
Chimichurri is one of the great sauces of the world — a simple, uncooked condiment of parsley, garlic, olive oil, vinegar, and herbs that originated in the Río de la Plata region of Argentina and Uruguay and became, across centuries of gaucho cattle culture, the inseparable partner of grilled beef. Its origins are debated with the kind of passionate disagreement that only truly important foods inspire. One popular etymology traces it to Basque immigrants — the Basque word tximitxurri meaning roughly a mixture of several things in no particular order — who arrived in Argentina in large numbers in the nineteenth century and brought their sheep-herding and meat-grilling traditions with them. Another theory traces it to an Englishman named Jimmy McCurry who allegedly distributed a similar herb sauce to Argentine soldiers during the wars of independence. Whatever its true origin, chimichurri became so deeply embedded in Argentine asado culture that to serve grilled beef without it is not merely unusual but almost culturally unthinkable. The classic green chimichurri — parsley-forward, sharp with vinegar, fragrant with oregano and garlic — is the most familiar version internationally, but red chimichurri, made with the addition of roasted red pepper, tomato, and often smoked paprika, is equally traditional and contributes a sweeter, more complex depth.

Chimichurri's arrival in American burger culture came through two routes simultaneously: the explosion of Argentine steakhouses in American cities beginning in the 1990s, and the broader trend toward Latin American flavors that transformed American restaurant menus across the same period. At Argentine parrillas — the wood-fired grill restaurants that became fashionable in New York, Los Angeles, and Miami — chimichurri was served in small clay pots alongside prodigious amounts of grilled beef, and American diners discovered it and wanted it on everything. Its translation to burgers was natural and immediate: the bright acid and fresh herb of the green chimichurri cut through the fat of ground beef the way lemon cuts through fried fish — not by suppressing the flavor but by releasing it, making it taste more fully like itself. Serving both green and red chimichurri on a single burger doubles the complexity and pays homage to the full tradition.

I spent three weeks in Buenos Aires one autumn, eating at parrillas every night with the kind of systematic dedication that I told myself was research and that was also simply the most enjoyable eating of my life. The beef in Argentina is extraordinary — grass-fed, loosely grazed on the vast pampas, with a flavor that is at once more mineral and more delicate than American grain-fed beef — and the chimichurri served alongside it was never quite the same twice. Every restaurant, every family, every neighborhood had its own version: more garlic here, less vinegar there, a particular ratio of flat-leaf to curly parsley, the addition of fresh cilantro in some places that purists considered scandalous. What they shared was a fundamental philosophy of freshness and brightness — sauce as a celebration of herbs and acid, not as a cover-up for inferior meat. Bringing that philosophy home and applying it to a burger was the most natural thing in the world.

Chimichurri on a burger is an argument in favor of medium rare in the most direct possible terms. The sauce is raw and alive — uncooked parsley and garlic and vinegar and olive oil, assembled without heat, retaining every molecule of freshness and brightness. To spoon it over a grey, well-done patty is to apply something vital and living to something that has already expired. To spoon it over a medium rare patty — pink at the center, moist with fat and juice, pulled from the heat at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit and rested properly — is to bring two living things together. The acid in the chimichurri makes the meat taste more like meat; the fat in the meat makes the chimichurri taste more like an herb garden. This is what cooking at medium rare makes possible: a conversation between two alive things, rather than a monologue.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
60g fresh flat-leaf parsley leaves and tender stems, very finely chopped
4 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
2 tbsp fresh oregano leaves, finely chopped (or 1 tsp dried)
1 large red bell pepper, roasted, peeled, and seeded (see method)
3 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
2 tbsp fresh oregano leaves, finely chopped
1 medium ripe tomato, seeded and finely diced
680g ground beef (80/20 chuck blend, grass-fed preferred)
4 slices provolone or mild Manchego cheese
1 small red onion, sliced into thin rounds
instructions: 1. Roast the red pepper: Place the red bell pepper directly over a gas burner flame on high, turning with tongs, until completely charred on all sides, about 10–12 minutes. Transfer to a bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and steam for 15 minutes. Peel, seed, and finely chop.

2. Make the green chimichurri: Combine parsley, garlic paste, oregano, and red pepper flakes in a bowl. Add red wine vinegar and olive oil and stir to combine. Season with salt and pepper. Let stand at room temperature at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours for the flavors to meld. Do not refrigerate — cold dulls the brightness.

3. Make the red chimichurri: Combine roasted red pepper, parsley, garlic paste, oregano, diced tomato, smoked paprika, and cayenne in a bowl. Add red wine vinegar and olive oil and stir to combine. Season with salt and pepper. Let stand at room temperature at least 30 minutes.

4. Make the bun dough: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix on medium with the dough hook for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
5. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.
6. Divide into 4 equal portions. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and let rise until doubled, about 45 minutes.
7. Brush buns with egg wash and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

8. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions of about 170g each. Form gently into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Refrigerate 15 minutes.
9. Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill pan over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side without pressing. Flip and cook 2–3 minutes second side.
10. Lay a slice of provolone or Manchego on each patty. Add a splash of water, cover immediately, and steam 30–45 seconds until cheese is melted.
11. Transfer patties to a resting rack and rest 3–4 minutes. Target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare.
12. Lightly brush red onion rounds with olive oil and cook in the hot skillet for 1–2 minutes per side until slightly charred. Set aside.
13. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

14. Assemble: Spoon 1 tablespoon of red chimichurri on the bottom bun. Place butter lettuce on top of the red chimichurri. Set the cheesed patty on the lettuce. Spoon 2 generous tablespoons of green chimichurri over the patty, letting it pool and drip around the edges. Add tomato slices and charred red onion rounds. Place a final small spoonful of red chimichurri on top. Finish with flaky sea salt. Set the top bun in place and serve immediately with extra chimichurri on the side.
